objectives: Run the whole Reader's Toolkit solo.
Track how a writer's feelings change from start to end.
Spot feelings that are shown, not told.
Use 3 new phrases: make an excuse, beginner's luck, sat up straighter.

learn.title: Brief: solo mission
learn.body:
Today's toolkit focus: **all of it, solo.** 🚀 No expert reader today: you run Predict, Clarify, Question, Infer and Summarise yourself.

Today's text is a **diary**. Diary writers often don't say "I was happy". They **show** it through what they did. So most diary questions are 🧠 **Work it out** questions about feelings, and feelings can **change** from the start to the end. Track them like a graph. 📈

⚠️ **Careful-reading trap:** one option today has the right words in the wrong order. Read every option to the end.

learn.title: 📚 Power words for today
items: **make an excuse** (phrase): give a reason, often not the real one, to get out of doing something. Use it: "He made an excuse to leave the boring party early."
**beginner's luck** (idiom): when someone new at something does well, people joke that it was just luck. Use it: "I won my first game of chess, and my brother said it was beginner's luck."
**sat up straighter** (body language): sitting up straight shows someone is suddenly alert, serious or determined. Use it: "When the teacher said 'test', the whole class sat up straighter."

learn.title: The diary: Hamza's diary
learn.body:
Thursday

Grandpa asked me to teach him my racing game today. I said yes, mostly because Mum was standing right behind him.

It was a disaster at first. He held the controller like it was a TV remote from the 1990s and kept steering with his whole body. Every time his car went left, Grandpa went left too, nearly off the sofa. He crashed into the same wall on the first bend nine times. I counted.

I was going to make an excuse and go to my room. Then, on the tenth try, he got round the bend. He didn't cheer. He just sat up straighter and said, "Again."

We played for two hours. I forgot to check my phone.

Around nine o'clock, he told me about the car he had when he was twenty. It was blue, it had no air conditioning, and he drove it from Amman to Aqaba with the windows down and sand in his teeth. He said the road was so empty he could see the heat shaking above it. I never knew Grandpa did anything except read the newspaper and fall asleep in front of the news.

By the end, he beat my time on the first track by half a second. I told him it was beginner's luck. He laughed so hard he had to take his glasses off.

Mum came in at ten and said it was time for bed. Neither of us moved.

Tomorrow he wants to try the mountain track. I've already set up the second controller.

learn.title: 🚀 Solo mission checklist
learn.body:
Before the challenges, run the whole toolkit yourself:

🔮 Was my prediction right?
🧐 Is there a word or phrase I should clarify?
🙋 What question would I ask Hamza?
🧠 How do Hamza's feelings change? Can I find one clue from the start and one from the end?
📝 Can I sum up the diary in one sentence?

If you can say yes to all five, you're reading like an expert. 🏆

check.prompt: 🔮 Predict: Today's text is "Hamza's diary", written by a boy who teaches his grandpa a video game. Which prediction fits a diary best?
check.hint: Think about the type of text. Who writes a diary, and what do they write about?
options: It will use "I" and tell us about Hamza's own day and feelings
It will be written by Grandpa, only about cars
It will be a news report about a gaming company
It will list the rules of the game
check.explanation: Diaries are written in the first person ("I") about the writer's own day and feelings. The text type is a big clue. After reading, check: was your prediction right? Good readers change their prediction as they go.

check.prompt: 🔤 Word detective: "It was a disaster at first." What does "disaster" mean here?
check.hint: This is a diary about playing a game with Grandpa. In that situation, what would a "disaster" be?
options: Something that went very badly
A big storm
A happy surprise
A type of car
check.explanation: Here "disaster" means something went very badly. It's an exaggeration: nobody got hurt, Grandpa just kept crashing in the game. Writers exaggerate to be funny.

check.prompt: 🔎 Find it: Where did Grandpa drive his blue car when he was twenty?
check.hint: Find the paragraph about the blue car. Check the order of the two places.
options: From Aqaba to Amman
From Amman to Aqaba
To the mountain track
To the newspaper office
check.explanation: From Amman to Aqaba. The first option has the right places in the wrong order: that's today's careful-reading trap.

check.prompt: 🧠 Work it out: At the start, why did Hamza agree to teach Grandpa?
check.hint: Read the second sentence. What does "mostly because Mum was standing right behind him" tell you about how keen he was?
options: He felt he had to, because his mum was watching
He was excited to play with Grandpa
Grandpa offered to pay him
He wanted to show off his best time
check.explanation: Clue: "mostly because Mum was standing right behind him". Think: he didn't really want to, but he couldn't say no in front of her. Being excited comes later in the diary, not at the start.

check.prompt: 🧩 Clue hunt: Which detail best shows that Hamza enjoyed the evening?
check.hint: Which detail would surprise you if a teenager wrote it about himself?
options: "I forgot to check my phone."
"He crashed into the same wall on the first bend nine times."
"Mum came in at ten and said it was time for bed."
"He held the controller like it was a TV remote from the 1990s."
check.explanation: A teenager who forgets his phone for two hours is having a great time. He never writes "I enjoyed it", but this detail shows it.

check.prompt: ✍️ Why did the writer...? Why does the writer end with "I've already set up the second controller"?
check.hint: Hamza set it up before anyone asked. What does that tell you about tomorrow?
options: To show, without saying it, that Hamza can't wait to play again
To explain how to connect a controller
To show that Hamza is annoyed
To tell us the game is broken
check.explanation: He got ready before anyone asked him to. That shows he's looking forward to tomorrow. The writer shows the feeling instead of naming it, which makes a strong ending.

check.prompt: 📝 Sum it up: In ONE sentence, what is this text mainly about? Start with: "This text is mainly about..."

markPoints.point: Says it's about Hamza teaching or playing the game with his grandpa

check.modelAnswer: This text is mainly about Hamza teaching his grandpa a racing game and enjoying it much more than he expected.
check.explanation: A good summary names WHO or WHAT the text is about and the MAIN thing that happens, in one sentence. Small details (numbers, colours, names of places) usually stay out.

check.prompt: 🙋 Your question: Write one Work it out question about the text: a question whose answer is NOT written in it.

markPoints.point: Asks a question that has to be worked out, not found (often starts with Why, How or What do you think)

check.modelAnswer: Why do you think Hamza never knew about Grandpa's blue car?
check.explanation: Asking your own questions is one of the strongest reading habits there is. A Find it question ("What colour was the car?") is too easy. A Work it out question makes you think: "Why...?", "How did he feel when...?", "What do you think...?"

check.prompt: 🧱 Use it: Write your own sentence using "beginner's luck". Make it about something in YOUR life, not about today's text.

markPoints.point: Uses "beginner's luck" with the right meaning (a new person doing well, joked to be just luck)

check.modelAnswer: The first time my cousin went bowling he got a strike, but we all said it was beginner's luck.
check.explanation: Using a new word in your own sentence is how it moves from "I've seen it" to "I own it". Check: does "beginner's luck" mean a new person doing well, joked to be just luck in your sentence?

practice.prompt: 🗂️ Sort it: Is each question about today's text Find it, Work it out, or Why did the writer...?
practice.hint: Ask yourself: could I point at the answer with my finger? If not, is it about the text, or about the writer's choices?

rows.statement: How many times did Grandpa crash on the first bend?
How did Hamza's feelings change during the evening?
rows.explanation: Not written. Clues: wanted to go to his room, then forgot his phone.

rows.statement: What colour was Grandpa's first car?
Why do you think Grandpa said "Again" instead of cheering?
rows.explanation: Not written. Clue: he sat up straighter. He was determined.

rows.statement: Why does the writer say "I counted" after the nine crashes?
rows.explanation: It's about the effect: it's funny and shows Hamza was bored and watching.

rows.statement: Why does the writer include the story about the blue car?
rows.explanation: It's about the effect: it shows Hamza seeing Grandpa in a new way.

practice.explanation: Find it = the answer is written in the text. Work it out = clue + think. Why did the writer = what a word or idea does to the reader.

practice.prompt: 💬 Own words: "Neither of us moved." What does this suggest about Hamza and Grandpa? Start with "This suggests that..." and use "because" to add your clue.

markPoints.point: They didn't want to stop / were enjoying it / had become close
Evidence: played two hours / forgot his phone / Grandpa laughed / mountain track tomorrow / ignored Mum

practice.modelAnswer: This suggests that they were enjoying the game so much that they didn't want to stop, because they had played for two hours, Hamza forgot his phone, and they even ignored Mum telling them to go to bed.
practice.explanation: One mark for the meaning (they didn't want to stop, they were enjoying it, they had become closer). One mark for proof from the diary (two hours, the phone, laughing, the mountain track).

summary: Diaries show feelings through actions, not labels.
Feelings can change: track them from start to end.
Careful reading: right words in the wrong order is still wrong.
👪 Talk card for a parent (2 minutes): "What's something an older relative taught you, or you taught them?" and "How did Hamza's feelings change?"

flashcards.back: Writers often show a feeling through actions (forgot his phone) instead of naming it (I was happy).
give a reason, often not the real one, to get out of something
a joke that a new person only did well because of luck
body language: suddenly alert, serious or determined
something that went very badly, often a funny exaggeration
